citeAs: Mihaylov, T., Clark, P., Khot, T., and Sabharwal, A. (2018). Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering. EMNLP 2018.
creator: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence; Heidelberg University)
description: OpenBookQA is a multiple-choice question answering dataset modeled after open book exams. It consists of approximately 5957 4-way multiple-choice questions paired with a set of 1326 elementary-level science facts (the "open book"). Answering the questions requires combining a core science fact from the open book with broad common knowledge, probing multi-hop reasoning and deeper understanding beyond simple retrieval.
name: OpenBookQA
rai:annotationsPerItem: 5 independent crowd-worker annotations per question (for answerability verification in Step 6 of the pipeline)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers from North America with a 'masters' level qualification. An in-house expert (Madeleine van Zuylen) provided additional annotation for Dev and Test questions.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was estimated using the 5 annotations collected per question during the answerability verification step. Using Hoeffding's Inequality, the estimated human accuracy H(Q) is at least ~H(Q) − 3% with probability over 98.8%. On Dev and Test sets (500 questions each), this yields a conservative human performance estimate of approximately 92%. An additional assessment on 100 randomly chosen questions from each of Train, Dev, and Test sets gave scores of 88.6%, 90.2%, and 91.6% respectively.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (workers from North America with a 'masters' level qualification)
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each crowd-worker was shown a random science fact f from set F, asked to think of a second common fact k that could be combined with f to derive a new valid assertion, then convert that assertion into a 4-way multiple-choice question with one correct answer and three incorrect distractors. The system verified basic checks (exactly 4 choices, no negation words, uniform answer choice length). The question was then fed to an IR solver and a word-association solver to verify hardness (neither should answer correctly and top 3 IR sentences should be insufficient). Five new crowd-workers then answered each question; if at least 4 of 5 answered correctly, it was deemed answerable. Answer choices were randomly shuffled to remove position bias. Dev and Test sets were additionally reviewed by an in-house expert.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly acknowledges human bias in crowdsourced datasets: (1) Answer position bias — before shuffling, choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions. (2) Plausible answer bias — certain answer choices are inherently more plausible for science questions (e.g., 'flying cats' is unlikely to be correct), exploitable by a choice-only model achieving ~50% accuracy. (3) Odd-one-out bias — incorrect answer choices tend to be homogeneous or share common properties uncharacteristic of the correct answer, since workers typically start with the correct answer and then generate three incorrect ones. These biases were partially mitigated by random shuffling of answer choices and by evaluating simple neural baselines to detect them early.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were created via a multi-stage crowdsourcing and partial expert filtering process. Workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk were shown a random science fact from the open book set F, asked to think of a second common fact that could be combined with it, then convert the combined assertion into a 4-way multiple-choice question. Questions were then filtered for hardness (must fool an IR solver and a word-association solver), answerability (at least 4 out of 5 crowd-workers must answer correctly), and answer-choice de-biasing (random shuffling). Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The core "open book" facts F consist of 1326 science facts drawn from a subset of the WorldTree corpus (Jansen et al., 2018), specifically from the 2287 WorldTree facts marked as "central" in at least one explanation, further filtered to those general enough to be applicable to multiple situations. Questions were generated by crowd-workers based on these facts.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web API, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The paper identifies several limitations: (1) In 21% of analyzed Train questions, the crowdsourced question does not actually require the original science fact to answer. (2) The auxiliary second-fact set K is noisy — facts are often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the question. (3) Even with oracle facts f and k, accuracy is only ~76%, far below human performance of ~92%, indicating non-trivial reasoning challenges remain. (4) Simple neural baselines can exploit annotation artifacts (plausible answer bias, odd-one-out bias) to achieve ~50% accuracy without reading the question. (5) The dataset focuses on a narrow domain (elementary science), limiting generalizability.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The open book facts F were filtered from 2287 WorldTree facts marked as "central" down to 1326 that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations. Questions were filtered for: (1) basic format checks (exactly 4 answer choices, no negation words, uniform answer choice length — all with at most 3 or at least 4 words); (2) hardness — must fool both an IR solver and a word-association solver, with top 3 IR retrieved sentences insufficient to answer; (3) answerability — at least 4 out of 5 crowd-workers must answer correctly (8140 questions collected, 2183 discarded in this step); (4) answer choice de-biasing via random shuffling; (5) expert review for Dev and Test splits.
rai:dataSocialImpact: OpenBookQA is intended to advance research on question answering systems that require multi-hop reasoning and integration of external knowledge, moving beyond simple pattern matching. The dataset highlights the large gap between current AI systems (~50% accuracy) and human performance (~92%), motivating further research on knowledge retrieval and reasoning for AI systems.
rai:dataUseCases: Open book question answering; evaluating multi-hop reasoning combining a provided science fact with broad common knowledge; benchmarking QA systems on elementary-level science questions; studying knowledge retrieval and reasoning in NLP systems.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: An IR solver (Clark et al., 2016) and a word-association based solver (Turney, 2017) were used during question generation to automatically verify hardness — questions were only kept if neither solver answered correctly and the top 3 IR retrieved sentences were insufficient to answer the question.
